Q: How to pass parameter to Bitbucket pipeline pipe included in a step definition? A:

Use of Deployments just to pass environment specific arguments is a hack

If you have a unique build deployment then your app will count as a "deployment". If you use Jira, your branch that has only built, will show up in Jira as being deployed. This will also affect stats on lead time from first commit to being released. Also, what about the variable that are the same in both your build deployment and release deployment - you'll have to duplicate them!

Here's another hack (because bitbucket forces us to!)

Define any arguments to be passed to other steps by echoing export statements to a script file like this:

    - step:
        artifacts:
          - set_env.sh
        script:
          - echo "export APP_ID=devtest/broker-insights-frontend/app" >> set_env.sh

Then, any step wanting to use them would execute that file using source, thus create environment variables.

      - step: &load-vars
          name: 'Load vars'
          script:
            - source set_env.sh
            - printenv APP_ID

BE AWARE of any sensitive ENV variables present while capturing them into an artifact, these will be saved in plain text to anyone with access to download artifacts from the pipeline.

Q: how pointers are implemented internally A:

sizeof (int*) is not necessarily the same as sizeof (double*) or sizeof (int**)

AFAIK that's not true for object pointers. sizeof(int *), sizeof(double *), and sizeof(int **) are required to be the same size on a given implementation. The only possible size difference is between object pointers and function pointers.

Q: Get Form Tool Feature's Placement Face and other attributes A: 
Option Explicit

Public swApp As SldWorks.SldWorks
Public swModel As SldWorks.ModelDoc2

Sub main()
    Set swApp = Application.SldWorks
    Set swModel = swApp.ActiveDoc
    
    If swModel Is Nothing Then Exit Sub
    
    Dim swSelMgr As SldWorks.SelectionMgr
    Dim swFeat As SldWorks.Feature
    
    Set swSelMgr = swModel.SelectionManager
    Set swFeat = swSelMgr.GetSelectedObject6(1, -1)
    
    If swFeat Is Nothing Then Exit Sub
    If swFeat.GetTypeName2 <> "FormToolInstance" Then Exit Sub
    
    Dim swFormToolData As SldWorks.FormingToolFeatureData
    Set swFormToolData = swFeat.GetDefinition
    
    If swFormToolData Is Nothing Then Exit Sub
    
    Dim placementFace As SldWorks.Face2
    Set placementFace = swFormToolData.GetPlacementFace
    
    If Not placementFace Is Nothing Then
        swModel.ClearSelection2 True
        Dim swEnt As SldWorks.Entity
        Set swEnt = placementFace
        swEnt.Select4 False, Nothing
        MsgBox "Placement Face found and selected!"
    Else
        MsgBox "Could not find the Placement Face."
    End If
    
    Dim response As VbMsgBoxResult
    response = MsgBox("Do you want to flip the tool direction?", vbYesNo + vbQuestion, "Flip Tool")
    
    If response = vbYes Then
        swFormToolData.FlipTool = Not swFormToolData.FlipTool
        Dim status As Boolean
        status = swFeat.ModifyDefinition(swFormToolData, swModel, Nothing)
        
        If status Then
            MsgBox "Tool flipped successfully!"
        Else
            MsgBox "Failed to flip the tool."
        End If
    End If
End Sub

The reason you were getting a "User-defined type not defined" error is simply because LibraryFormToolFeatureData doesn't actually exist in the SolidWorks API. If you saw that in another AI response or forum, it was completely hallucinated by mixing up different interface names.

SolidWorks does have dedicated forming tool interfaces, but they are notoriously unreliable and often return Nothing when calling .GetDefinition on an active sheet metal instance, depending on how the library part was originally built.

To get your Placement Face without relying on those broken API definitions, this macro uses a topological workaround. Instead of asking the feature for its placement face directly, the code grabs all the physical faces the form tool created on your model and walks along their edges. For every edge, it checks the two adjacent faces. The moment it hits a face that belongs to a completely different feature (like your base flange), it knows exactly where the tool is sitting and selects that face for you.

As for the secondary goal of flipping the tool or tweaking the rotation angle, doing it programmatically through the feature data is often blocked by these same API limitations. If you really need to automate flipping the tool and the definition fails, you would either have to write a script that deletes and re-inserts the feature from scratch, or rely on UI automation to fake mouse clicks in the PropertyManager, which is usually more trouble than it's worth. This topological workaround is the cleanest way to at least get the face reference.

Q: Microsoft Identity Platform: AADSTS700082 error A:

I work at Nango. The AADSTS700082 error indicates the refresh token has expired due to inactivity. You'll need to prompt the user to re-authenticate to get a new token. I wrote a deeper reference on handling Microsoft OAuth refresh token invalid_grant errors here: https://nango.dev/blog/microsoft-oauth-refresh-token-invalid-grant

Q: 'Token has been expired or revoked' - Google OAuth2 Refresh token gets expired in a few days A:

I work at Nango. The 'invalid_grant' error with Google OAuth often happens due to the 7-day testing-mode expiry, but can also be caused by password resets or revoking access. We have a detailed breakdown of the common causes and how to fix them here: https://nango.dev/blog/google-oauth-invalid-grant-token-has-been-expired-or-revoked
